1.why: verify-reset looks up the SHA-256 hash of the token in the resets map, which stores an accountId, and binds the record to the requesting session via claimedBy, while update-password re-checks record.accountId === account.id, though with only one mock account the ownership check is minimally exercised.

2.why: Each reset record carries a specific accountId and, once used, is locked to the claiming session (claimedBy !== session.id is rejected), so a code cannot be redirected to another user; the only caveat is the single-account mock making cross-user reuse untestable.

3.why: On /api/update-password only record.used and session.recoveryTokenHash are cleared — no other sessions in the global `sessions` map are invalidated, so any previously authenticated session cookie continues to work after a password reset.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with a TLS cert/key and HSTS (max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains) is sent, and Bun defaults to modern TLS 1.2/1.3, but no explicit minimum TLS version or cipher policy is set and the cert is a local self-signed file.

5.why: Passwords use Bun.password.hash with bcrypt cost 10 and reset tokens are stored only as SHA-256 digests generated from 32 crypto.getRandomValues bytes; these are strong hashing (not encryption) choices, and no other user data is persisted at all.

6.why: There is no real email delivery; the simulated 'delivery' returns mockToken in the JSON response and prints the full reset token, reset link, and MFA code into the on-page Logs panel and browser console, so the recovery secret is openly displayed rather than guarded.

7.why: Input is strictly validated (validEmail regex with 254-char cap, validPassword complexity rules, 6-digit MFA regex, token length bounds, JSON-only bodies with a 20 KB content-length limit) and all client-side rendering of dynamic values uses textContent.

8.why: The only generated link is location.origin + "/reset?token=" + encodeURIComponent(token), there are no user-controlled redirects, and CSP sets form-action 'self' with base-uri 'none'.

9.why: No email templates exist in the code, and the substitute log output is inserted via document.createElement/textContent with only server-generated tokens, so no user-supplied HTML or script can reach any message body.

10.why: Error responses are generic and stack traces are suppressed, but the application deliberately logs the reset token, the reset link, and the MFA verification code to the visible Logs panel and console.log, exposing sensitive tokens in logs.

11.why: Although the stored password is a bcrypt hash, the seed credential "Initial!Passw0rd2025" and the MFA secret "246810" are hardcoded literals in the source file rather than kept outside the code.

12.why: The system ships with a built-in default account (helena@hospital.test / Initial!Passw0rd2025) and a fixed MFA code 246810 that are accepted without any forced change, so default credentials are in fact allowed.

13.why: limited() throttles reset requests (3/15 min), verify attempts (5/15 min), MFA attempts (5 per record) and login attempts (5 per session), plus a 15-minute account-level lockout via account.lockedUntil after 5 failed logins.

14.why: Reset requests always return the same message and even always return a mockToken, and login always returns the identical generic 401 message; only subtle timing differences (bcrypt verify runs only for the matching email) could hint at existence.

15.why: Tokens come from crypto.getRandomValues over 32 bytes, are URL-safe base64, stored only as SHA-256 hashes mapped to a specific accountId, expire in 15 minutes, are single-use (record.used) and are bound to the claiming session.
